note: Found from the wrong end. hooks/before_bash.py refused a commit whose message merely named NESTOR_SEAL_KEY in prose, because the message was a heredoc piped to tail: lexed whole, the body's words were flattened into the last pipeline stage, and _is_secret_path matched the substring -- agent-log §6.38's raw-match-inside-longer-text, applied to something that was never an argument. Investigating that false positive turned up the same gap running the other way. Nothing ever scanned a body as code, so `bash <<'X' ... cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa ... X` reached no rule at all; nor did `echo '...' | sh` (the fetch-piped-to-shell rule only fired after a fetcher) or `bash < payload.sh`. `sh -c '...'` was unwrapped and re-scanned; every route where a shell takes its script from stdin was not. The guard reported on the visible half of a command while the executed half went unread.

decisions.question: What is a heredoc body to a command scanner?
decisions.commitment: Data, and only data, unless something executes it. _strip_heredocs separates body from command before lexing, so body words never reach the argument rules. A shell fed by a heredoc gets its body re-scanned as commands, because the text is right there in the payload -- scan it rather than guess. Verified across 16 cases before and after, and end to end through the real hooks/nestor-hook wrapper.
decisions.why: The scanner was treating the body as both and neither: as arguments, where it produced false refusals, and never as code, where it mattered. One missing model produced both symptoms, so modelling it fixes both -- and the fix that only silenced the false positive would have left the bypass, while arguably making it easier to reach.

decisions.question: A shell can also take its script from a pipe or a file. What then?
decisions.commitment: Refuse. `echo '...' | sh` runs whatever the left-hand side prints and `bash < payload.sh` runs a file that may not exist yet; neither is readable at hook time. sh -c '...' stays allowed because it is scannable and already re-scanned. No `| sh`, `| bash`, or `bash <` appears anywhere in the tree, so the new refusals break no documented workflow.
decisions.why: A guard that cannot read what will run should say so rather than stay quiet. Allowing the unscannable case is worse than refusing it, because the allow is indistinguishable from a scan that found nothing -- which is exactly how three bypasses sat open without anyone noticing.

decisions.question: The false positive came from _is_secret_path matching a bare identifier. Narrow it?
decisions.commitment: No. The predicate is untouched. Requiring a slash or an extension would have cleared the false positive and stopped catching `cat seal_key`. What moved is what the predicate is applied to, not how strict it is, and a test pins that `cat seal_key`, `cat ~/.nestor/seal_key`, `strings sean_seal_key.pem` and `tail -5 ~/.ssh/id_rsa` are all still refused.
decisions.why: The obvious fix for a noisy rule is to make the rule quieter, and in a secret-read guard that trades a false positive for a false negative -- the direction that fails silently. When a guard is noisy, suspect what it is being pointed at before suspecting what it is looking for.

decisions.question: What does this say about how the gates get audited?
decisions.commitment: That a gate's false positives are worth following. This bypass was open with tests passing, hook_guard reporting all five blocking gates proven, and nobody looking -- it surfaced only because the same defect also produced a visible nuisance. The six new tests in tests/test_before_bash.py assert the refusals as well as the allow, so the bypass cannot reopen quietly.
decisions.why: hook_guard proves each gate denies the case it was written for; it cannot prove a gate sees every route to that case. A rule that is never exercised from an unexpected direction is a rule nobody has actually checked -- and the agent tripping over the noise is the cheapest signal that direction exists.
